utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Good afternoon to everybody in the courtroom. As you can see, we are only two Judges present today. Judge Nyambe is not in a position to attend court hearings this week so that the remaining Judges decided to sit pursuant to Rule 15 bis. I think it is worth to note that we will hear today the 100th witness of the Prosecution. That is a remarkable progress. On the other hand, it shows that we have still quite a lot to do ahead, and we should speed up as much as possible. The Chamber's always interested in an expeditious but fair trial. Is there anything to raise before the witness will be brought in? Mr. Gajic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, concerning two documents used during cross-examination of Mr. Momir Nikolic, OTP witness, we selected a certain number of pages from Momir Nikolic's interview provided to the OTP under separate 65 ter numbers. They were uploaded in e-court as such, and we seek to tender them now. The relevant pages from document 65 ter 7274 are in 65 ter 1D730. And the relevant pages of 65 ter number 7280 are now a separate document in e-court under 65 ter number 1D731. The relevant portion of 65 ter document 1D211, which was used during cross-examination of Sir Rupert Smith, another OTP witness, is something that the Defence included in a separate document which is now 65 ter number 1D735. Concerning that document, we singled out around 20 pages in e-court which had been taken out of the previous document. Defence would also like to ask the Chamber to have them admitted into evidence, 1D730, 1D731, and 1D735.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Gajic, during the first break the registrar will liaise with you and check these different numbers. I just want to raise one matter. The pages -- the 20 pages you now indicated and have uploaded into e-court of the document tendered with Sir Rupert Smith is -- we have already the document D48 in evidence, which is also a part of that document. It could be preferable to attach these pages of this document you are referring to to this document D48, but I think again you should contact the registry during the first break and then we find the best way to avoid any problems and errors on numbering. Do you agree to that? Mr. Gajic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President. We accept your suggestion, of course. A brief remark only: D48 does not include the pages included in 1D211. Of course, we absolutely accept your suggestion, because these are all parts of the same book, although it presents two different points of view.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: As D48 is also a Defence exhibit, it would be better to attach the new pages to that previous document so that everything you tendered would be in evidence. We leave it until after the break. The witness should be brought in, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir. Welcome to the courtroom. Would you please read aloud the affirmation on the card which is shown to you now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Please sit down and make yourself comfortable. As you know, you will be now interrogated by the parties, first by the Prosecution. Mr. Vanderpuye has questions for you. Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, and good afternoon to you, Your Honours. Good afternoon to everyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And good afternoon to you, Mr. Todorovic. As I told you last week when we met, I do have a fair number of questions to put to you. I just want to remind you to try and speak a little bit more slowly than you would otherwise so that you and I can be understood by the interpreters for the benefit of all the parties, and if there's anything that I ask you during the course of this examination that's not clear to you, please let me know and I'll see if there's a way that I can phrase it in a manner that we can better understand one another.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters note: Could the witness please be asked to move closer to the microphone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Sir, would you please move a little bit further to the microphone so the interpreters can listen to you better. Thank you very much. Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Todorovic, could you please state your full name for the record and spell your surname?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC
utterances.text: My name is Milenko Todorovic, T-o-d-o-r-o-v-i-c.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And, Mr. Todorovic, what is your age, and where were you born?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC
utterances.text: I was born on the 27th of December, 1947, in the village of Gornja Krcina.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I know that you have some concerns about testifying here today. Are you here today voluntarily, or are you here because you were otherwise required to be here?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC
utterances.text: I am in this courtroom for the first time. However, last year, in late January or early February, I was summoned to appear to the Tribunal office in Belgrade for an interview concerning my duties and tasks as the chief of the intelligence and security organ in the East Bosnia Corps. I was advised of my status if it became necessary for me to appear before this Tribunal and the procedure under the law as such.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: As you've mentioned the interview which occurred at the Belgrade field office, was that interview conducted on the 2nd and the 3rd of February, 2010, to your recollection?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Can I consult the transcript? I have the date there, but I think those are the dates, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. And to our knowledge, was that interview tape recorded?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC
utterances.text: As far as I remember, I was asked whether I accept for it to be recorded, and I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Now, you've indicated that you have that statement there in your bag. Have you had an opportunity to read the transcript of -- rather, the interview, not the statement. Have you had an opportunity to read the transcript of the interview before coming here to testify today?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I have had an opportunity to read it. I received it around ten days ago by post.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And when did you review it, about ten days ago or -- or some other time?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: The witness received it by e-mail.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When I opened the attachment to the message, I read it and it took me about an hour or two.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And you read the transcript of that interview in your own language; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Having read the transcript, Mr. Todorovic, does it fairly and accurately reflect what you said during the course of the interviews on the 2nd and 3rd of February of 2010?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC
utterances.text: In principle it does, to the best of my recollection. It does reflect the interview conducted with me in Belgrade. I have no serious objections as to its contents.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I take it then that you stand by what you said during the course of that interview.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I just would like to get a bit of background information from you before I get into the substance of your testimony, and what I'd like to focus on first is a bit of your professional background. Are you currently working?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC
utterances.text: No. I am not employed. I am retired. I retired in -- I'm not sure. 2002 or 2003.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And at that time, what did you retire from? What kind of work were you doing?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC
utterances.text: I retired from the army. I was in the same position that I performed until then, and I retired with the rank of colonel.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And prior to joining the -- first of all, was -- did you retire from the Army of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. My last position was chief of the security department of the 3rd Corps command of the VRS in Bijeljina. However, it was under the 30th Personnel Centre of the then VJ.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Prior to joining the VRS, were you a member of the JNA?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was. I was an active duty member of the JNA since the 20th of July, 1966.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Can you briefly just outline, if you would, or list the positions that you had during your career with the JNA before you joined the VRS.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC
utterances.text: In 1966, I completed the military high school, which was an NCO school. I specialised in artillery. After that, I was assigned to Slovenska Bistrica near Maribor in Slovenia. I -- while working in the JNA, I continued my education, and I received my first commissioned officer rank of 2nd lieutenant in 1971. After that, because of the needs of the service, I was transferred to the garrison in Ljubljana and then to Ribnica, which is also a small town nearby Ljubljana. My position was battery commander, following which I returned from Ribnica to Slovenska Bistrica, also as a battery commander. Next, in Slovenska Bistrica I was assigned to a staff position as a desk clerk for educational affairs in the command of the artillery regiment. In 1983, I was sent to the security school in Pancevo because such were the needs of the service, and I agreed to that transfer. I completed that school there, following which I returned and was assigned as the security organ in the garrison in Ptuj, P-t-u-j. From the garrison, I was sent to the garrison in Maribor, to the division command. There, too, I was in the security organ. In 1985, I left the security service, which was not of my own volition, but I was appointed commander of the artillery regiment in Slovenska Bistrica. I remained in that position for three years, whereupon I met the conditions for further education in the General Staff school. In 1988, I handed over the duty of the regiment commander to go back to the security service. That was in 1988 when I returned to the security service. A year later, 1989, I was sent to the General Staff school in Belgrade for further education, and I took general courses. I completed the school in 1991, in June. Having graduated from the General Staff school, I was assigned to a duty with the security administration of the General Staff of the VJ -- or, rather, of the Ministry of Defence. I remained there until my departure for the VRS in mid-November 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: When you were assigned to the VRS in mid-November 1993, to what position -- what position did you take up there?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC
utterances.text: It was called a temporary assignment. I was sent to serve with the VRS and assigned to the position of chief of intelligence and security department of the command of the East Bosnian Corps, the headquarters of which were in Bijeljina.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I see the transcript reads that you were assigned as the chief of the intelligence security department of the command of the East Bosnia Corps. Did you also serve the function or was it also your position that you were the assistant commander for the security and intelligence in that corps?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC
utterances.text: It is the same thing, basically. At certain commander levels, positions can be that of assistant commanders for intelligence and security, and at the same time the person in charge is also chief of the security and intelligence department or organ, and that term may vary depending on the level of command. In any case, it is in direct line of subordination to the unit commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: How did it come about that you were assigned to the East Bosnia Corps in 1993?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC
utterances.text: You mean in the technical sense or -- I'm not quite clear what you mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Well, you indicated that prior to that you were serving in Belgrade; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. And so how is it that you -- not in a technical sense but in a factual sense, how is it you wound up at the East Bosnia Corps in the position that you held?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC
utterances.text: In the then JNA, the practice was for professional commissioned and non-commissioned officers who were born in Bosnia and Herzegovina and Croatia were temporarily assigned to the units of the Army of Republika Srpska or the Army of the Serbian Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And prior to your transfer to the East Bosnia Corps, did you discuss that with anyone?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC
utterances.text: I was told, just like my other colleagues were, that it would be an ethical, moral thing to respond to this call and that that is what we were trained for during our professional education and that we should take up the corresponding duty in those units. Specifically for this post, I had an interview or conversation with the then chief of the administration, of the security administration of the Army of Yugoslavia, General Dimitrijevic, and with General Tolimir, who asked me -- but, actually, they didn't ask me, because by their position they were superior to me, both Tolimir and General Dimitrijevic. I was of lower rank, but I was told that the cadre situation was unfavourable, that there were many vacancies in the intelligence and security organ of the East Bosnia Corps command and that if I were appointed to that post that would contribute to the personal and professional resolution of that particular issue. I accepted that, even though I did state that I had some medical difficulties myself, as well as in my family, but I still agreed to take up these duties.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Did you have -- I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC
utterances.text: I would like to emphasise that during my service, particularly during the wartime years, a lot of understanding was shown for my personal and my family situation, and if it was every necessary for me or for my family, my wife, to go for medical check-ups, there were no problems. My wife was also suffering from some medical difficulties. All the more so because Bijeljina is not that far from Belgrade, some 130 kilometres away from Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: In terms of your assignment to the East Bosnia Corps and the discussions you had, did you have those discussions in particular with General Tolimir?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, briefly. He was with General Dimitrijevic, the chief of the Army of Yugoslavia's security and intelligence administration. Until then we didn't know each other personally. Later on I found out that General Tolimir served for a while in Macedonia, in Dalmatia, in Split, in Knin. I was serving my duties in a completely different part of the former Yugoslavia, so before then we didn't know each other personally. That's why the conversation was very short, because at that time, we didn't really have any topics that we needed to discuss at any length.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I take it, then, that the conversation you had with General Tolimir at that time in 1993 was in person, that is, face-to-face. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And do you know how it is that he came to pick you in particular for the position at the East Bosnia Corps?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Well, I never asked him about it, but I assume that he could see the personnel files that were with the chief and that he could see there where I was born, also my professional qualifications for that particular duty and that on the basis of that they concluded that I was from that area and that I was the most suitable for that particular post.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: The East Bosnia Corps in particular, if you could just describe where it is situated -- or where it was situated, shall we say, when you got there in 1993.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC
utterances.text: The East Bosnia Corps command or the command as the organisational unit was located at the entrance to Bijeljina as you're coming from the Sremska-Raca direction. It's the north-eastern entrance to Bijeljina. Thus there were a few private houses that were requisitioned through the Ministry of Defence for the requirements of the army, and that's where the corps command was located.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I'd just like to show you 65 ter 1454, please. If we could -- well, first, tell me if you recognise what you see here?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC
utterances.text: I see a geographical map of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and I recognise it as such. Geographically and territorially.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. I'd just like to blow up the portion where it's written "East Bosnia Corps." And you can see a flag that is where it's written underneath it "Bijeljina." Is that roughly, or can you confirm if that's roughly the area where the command would have been situated in that area?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Maybe we can blow it up a little bit more so the witness can see it more clearly.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's it. If we had the city map, I could show you the houses and each street individually, but in view of the scale of this map, I think it is correctly shown, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Could you give us an approximation, if you know, of the distance it is between, say, Zvornik and Bijeljina?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC
utterances.text: I think it's about 53 or 54 kilometres. Between 50 and 55 kilometres, actually.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. All right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And I'm done with this exhibit for the moment. Then I would like to tender the map. I understand the map is not admitted yet in evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 65 ter document 1454 shall be assigned Exhibit Number P2179. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Mr. Todorovic -- or would you prefer to be addressed as Colonel Todorovic? Let me know.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Whatever you prefer. I was a colonel when I was working. Now I'm just a regular citizen, a retired person, but I have nothing against you using that rank. I still have the rank. I haven't lost it.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. Colonel, when you arrived at the East Bosnia Corps in November 1993, I just want to get a very basic idea of what the structure or the organisation of the corps was like then, but who was the commanding officer, the commander of the corps, at that time?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC
utterances.text: The corps structure -- actually, I'll begin from the corps command, and I'll do it briefly. If you need any more details, I'll be happy to do it like that. The corps commander, General Major Novica Simic was the commander of the corps. His deputy and the Chief of Staff at the same time was Colonel at the time and later General Budimir Gavric. His assistant, the East Bosnia Corps assistant for logistics, was Colonel Petar Stojanovic. The assistant for morale, religious, and so on and so forth, was Colonel Slobodan Jelacic. And the assistant or the chief of the intelligence and security section was retired Colonel Jovanovic. Actually, it's not Jovanovic. It's Petar Jakovljevic, Petar Jakovljevic, whom I took over from when I arrived. The chief of the security force -- of the intelligence and security organ, and at the same time the assistant commander for intelligence and security affairs.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Can you tell us who was the commander for the military police battalion of the corps. That would be the 3rd Military Police Battalion.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC
utterances.text: The military police battalion commander of the East Bosnia Corps, which became the 3rd Corps or the 3rd Battalion of the military police after the war was at that time Captain Dragisa Vulin. Later he was a major, but I think now that he is a colonel and that he's also retired. So when I went there in 1993, the commander of the military police battalion was Captain Dragisa Vulin.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And was Captain Vulin in that position in 1995, as well as General Simic and General Gavric?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. They were there until the end, and until the time that I left from the East Bosnia Corps until 1997, because that's when I went back to the Army of Yugoslavia, in 1997, from the East Bosnia Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: As the assistant commander for security and intelligence in the command from 1993 through the end of the war, who was your immediate superior within the security chain?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC
utterances.text: My immediate superior was the commander of the unit in whose composition we belonged. So my immediate superior was General Novica Simic. And this was the principle in the Army of Yugoslavia and the Army of Republika Srpska. However, there is a kind of difference between the organs of security and intelligence. There is a professional line of command and control. It's a professional line of command and direction. According to that professional line of directing, my immediate superior was General Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Gajic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I think on page 14, lines 17 to 20, are not translated in the best possible way. It's not quite what the witness said, so I would like to ask the Prosecutor to repeat his question.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I have no problem. Thank you. I'll do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: My question was: In the security chain, who was your immediate superior?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC
utterances.text: In my answer, I was a little broader, so first I emphasised that my general superior was the military commander, and then in the second part of my answer I answered your question. Along the security professional line, my immediate superior was General Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I'd like to take you to a different area, and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: May I ask a question to this matter, which there is one thing I didn't understand very clearly. You said your position was assistant commander for intelligence and security, and at the same time as chief of the intelligence and security department or unit. Can you tell me what is the difference between the two positions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There isn't really a difference between those two posts. Just as in the intelligence, security section whose chief I was, and at the same time on my work labour card under "Personal data," it states that at the same time I was assistant commander for intelligence and security. This means that I was doing the intelligence security organ's duties such as gathering and compilation of data, providing proposals, providing them to the commander for his review, and to my superior according to the security chain of command. I don't know if I was clear enough.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: The term "chief" refers to your position you held in the -- in this unit, and the term "assistant commander" referred to your relation to your superiors or how can I understand it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm trying to find an adequate way to explain. The chief of the security and intelligence department is, at the same time - you could say this was a dual function - also the assistant commander for intelligence and security affairs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Assistant to whom?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] To the corps commander. To the corps commander or the commander in whose command you are. So if we're talking about the East Bosnia Corps command, I was the chief of the intelligence and security organ there and at the same assistant commander for intelligence and security affairs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. That clarifies the situation. Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. If it's of any benefit to the Court, I plan to get into some of the more detailed functions of his position a little bit later on in the examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I was intending to take you to a different area, in particular to July 1995. First, Colonel, do you recall about when it was that the Srebrenica enclave fell in July of 1995?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC
utterances.text: During the interview in Belgrade, I really couldn't remember the precise date. I know it was sometime in mid-June. However, now from the transcript and all of this I see and I accept that this was actually on the 11th of July or the 12th that this happened. It's been a while since then. Sixteen years almost since that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I just want to clarify one thing that's in the record at page 16, line 23. You're recorded as having said, and it may be erroneous, but you're recorded as having said, "I know it was sometime in mid-June."

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC
utterances.text: It's probably not correctly translated. I don't know. It was either my slip of the tongue when I was pronouncing the month then and now. Actually, I didn't think then, nor do I think now that it was June but that it was July.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you for that clarification, Colonel. Can you recall -- or can you explain how it is you came to learn of the fall of Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC
utterances.text: When we talked about that in Belgrade, I said then, and now I'm saying that as well, that I cannot really be precise as to whether I learned about it in the corps command or if I learned about it through the media. The time period since then has been considerable. I don't remember whether I had left and gone home and then three hours later I learned about it. The work hours were 24 hours a day. We even slept at our jobs. So I cannot really say whether I heard it at the command when it was already all over, or if I learned about it from the media, because they were broadcasting or announcing important information from the front.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Around that time did you receive any tasks concerning prisoners?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I cannot really be specific about the date. I couldn't do it in Belgrade, I cannot do it now, as to whether that was on the same day in the evening or the following day or two days later, but in any case, it was after the fall of Srebrenica, I think, and I am 90 per cent sure that a telegram came from the Main Staff that the East Bosnia Corps command should be engaged and should prepare accommodation at the Batkovic collection centre for another 1.000 to 1.200 -- 1.100 or 1.200. So 1.000 to 1.200, as far as I can remember. Thus to prepare accommodation for new detainees who are going to be coming over the coming days. I immediately informed the corps commander. He took further steps through his other assistants, through the logistics sector and others for these preparations to be actually carried out.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Now, you've indicated here that you're 90 per cent sure that you received a telegram from the Main Staff at the East Bosnia Corps command. First, do you remember from whom that telegram came?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC
utterances.text: I did say that I am convinced 90 per cent that it was a telegram, and I said that because when we were talking in Belgrade, there was a dilemma as to whether I was informed by phone or whether this was in a personal contact between myself and General Tolimir about this particular assignment. So I attempted to go over everything, and I'm sure that it was not done in personal contact, and I said that I was 90 per cent sure that it was a telegram from the Main Staff which, according to my recollection, was signed by Tolimir. Well, I could be mistaken, but probably this telegram exists somewhere in the archives.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Do you have any doubt as you're testifying here today as to whether or not this task you were assigned came from General Tolimir?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Well, you know, when you don't have any documents -- I don't even have any of my working notes, because when I left my post, I handed them in, and they have been destroyed. I don't have that telegram in front of me in order to be able to say, yes, I do recognise it. Then the memory after 16 years, you know how it is. It can be deceptive, and I wouldn't want to err on one side or the other and be decisive about it and say 1.000 per cent this or that and be wrong. As far as my recollection serves me, it is what is said how it was without any intention.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Do you remember what you said during the course of your interview in February 2010?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Well, the sense of it is what we're saying now, what I'm saying now. I don't remember every single word.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Well, maybe if I read a little bit of it to you it will help refresh your recollection.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, please do, and then we will.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: On page 37 of the transcript of your interview --

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Just a moment and I'll get the proper identifying number for the Trial Chamber. Mr. President, this is a document that doesn't have a 65 ter number, but insofar as I'm using it to refresh the witness's recollection, I'm not offering it into evidence at this point anyway. At page -- it is listed as a statement, obviously, on his list of statements as I've given that to the Trial Chamber. It's connected or attached to the list of exhibits.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Is it uploaded into e-court?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: It appears it's on the Defence exhibit list, and it's 1D733.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Gajic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I think that it would be a good thing to show the witness this document. It's in the e-court, and the number is 1D733, pursuant to 65 ter Rule.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Vanderpuye. We have it on the screen. In English the first page, I think, interview of the 2nd of February. Now we turn to the relevant pages.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: We have page 37 in the English, and I don't have the reference for the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: The court usher is trying to find the relevant page. Mr. Gajic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I think the relevant page in the Serbian is 35.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: What we have in the English, Mr. President, about midway through the page, is a question that's put to the witness during the course of the interview, which is: "Ok, are you certain or not certain that the information came from General Tolimir, whether it was in person or by telegram?" And the answer is: "I am sure about that."

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Does that refresh your recollection as to whether the information you received concerning that task came from General Tolimir?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC
utterances.text: I can see the text before me, and I do not dispute that I said so at the time. What I said a moment ago, in my view, is not considerably different. In any case, I did underscore that before me I have neither my notebook nor the telegram so as to be able to say precisely whether it was in a telegram or in some other form, that message which arrived from Tolimir. In any case, I'm certain that I spoke with General Tolimir on the phone when we discussed when they would be coming. Then I was informed by him to drop the task and stop any further preparations, but I don't think we've gone that far yet. That's why I'm saying that I am 90 per cent sure, looking from this place, that it was by way of a telegram, and I believe I received it from the intelligence and security administration, and the chief of that administration was General Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Do you recall saying during the course of your interview that you could not exclude the possibility that you met face-to-face with General Tolimir in relation to this task?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC
utterances.text: We discussed that situation in Belgrade at length, but I arrived at the interview without knowing what the topics would be specifically. Therefore, I was unable to recollect many things off-the-cuff. It's been a long time ago, and now I have to say whether this happened this way or that. I remember the gist of it, but I am uncertain about the details. So the gist of it, which is not in dispute, is that I am 90 per cent sure that I received a telegram rather than a phone call when I learned that we needed to set up accommodation for those 1.000 to 1.200 prisoners. And I believe it also arrived to my service through code, and if it arrived in such a way, it came from the intelligence and security administration, headed by General Tolimir. I received all important information through the professional line, and I was duty-bound to inform of all such information to General Simic, my corps commander. I was also supposed to pass on to him any tasks and instructions which came from the superior command.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Tell us in detail, as best as you can recall it, what the task was that you were assigned in relation to the prisoners that you spoke about just after the fall of Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Do you mean my conversations with General Simic or General Tolimir?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: If you had a conversation with General Tolimir about the task that you were assigned when you were assigned it, I'd like to know what it was that you were told to do.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Concerning that task, which, as I say, I'm 90 per cent sure arrived by way of a telegram, I did not have a conversation with General Tolimir. I informed General Simic, the corps commander. I told him that a telegram had arrived. I showed it to him and told him that we should start our preparations and we did.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: What did the telegram say, Colonel?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC
utterances.text: It's difficult to say even approximately. I can't quote it, but it was something to the effect that for those 1.000 to 1.200 prisoners to be accommodated, who were members of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina from Srebrenica, should be accommodated, and that accommodation provided by the corps command. It was also stated that they should be placed at Batkovic. That was the contents of the telegram, more or less.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: You indicated you relayed this to your commander; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: What did you tell your commander?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC
utterances.text: I showed him the telegram so he could read it. I placed it in his hands. I didn't make any particular comment.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: What did you do?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC
utterances.text: I didn't do anything. It was the commander who ordered the respective organs to carry out preparations. Personally, I had no other obligations regarding it.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I didn't ask you about obligations. I asked you what did you do in relation to that task that was directed to you.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC
utterances.text: I received it to be relayed to the corps commander so that they could do it. I don't know why it arrived in the security department. It is possible that some other assistant commanders at the Main Staff were absent and then perhaps General Tolimir took it upon himself to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I appreciate that you're trying to be helpful, Colonel, but I asked you a very specific question, and I would appreciate it if you could give us a specific answer. I'm going to ask my question again. What did you do in relation to the task that came to you from General Tolimir?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC
utterances.text: As I said, I'm not sure if we understood each other though, that I informed the commander by placing the telegram in his hands, and I have in mind the corps commander. Since the collection centre at Batkovic is directly subordinated to the corps commander, the corps commander issued specific orders to his other subordinates to implement what was requested of them in the telegram in order to make preparations to receive the prisoners and my job was finished. Practically speaking, I simply transmitted the telegram from the Main Staff, which was received by the security organ, to the corps commander for further action. I'm not holding anything back. I'm telling you everything about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: What preparations were required to be made to receive these prisoners, a thousand, 1.300 prisoners at the Batkovic camp?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC
utterances.text: The collection centre, or as it sometimes was referred to as the Batkovic camp, was in the environs of Bijeljina, close to the Batkovic village, so actually it was some 10 to 15 kilometres away from Bijeljina. It was part of an agricultural compound. There were a number of hangars there which were used for different purposes such as to store wheat, to store fertilisers, agricultural machinery and everything else that would be needed by a farm or an agricultural facility. Some of them were empty, and there had already been established a reception centre and that it could house several hundred people. In any case, this figure was now greater, which required the machinery and wheat to be taken out. Water pipes had to be put in place, outdoor toilets set up, as well as other preparations which were required to provide the basic conditions. However, none of that was under my competence. It was the corps command logistics branch which had to take upon themselves all those tasks issued by the corps commander. That is why I say that I had no further obligations towards the task.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Did you go there to inspect the premises in relation to these preparations?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC
utterances.text: No, I did not, because there were numerous military and security problems continually along the lines, and myself and all of my security organs were constantly engaged performing corps tasks. Perhaps at a later point I believe I did go to see it, but not at that point in time.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: When did you go to see it?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Again, I'm uncertain about the date. Sometime later, perhaps a month later when a group of about 170 or 180 captured members of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina from the area of the Zvornik Brigade was brought to Batkovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Did these thousand prisoners, 1.300 prisoners, ever arrive at the camp?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC
utterances.text: No, it never did. Can I offer a comment?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC
utterances.text: At that period of time, there were many members of East Bosnia Corps who were captured by the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and they were placed in a similar camp or holding centre in the area of Tuzla. Their relatives, parents, friends, when they learned through the media, and information also leaked from commands, that there were between 10- and 1.200 prisoners from the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina arriving at Batkovic, they basically besieged the commanders of the VRS units where their family members had served in inquiring why those people from Srebrenica were still not arriving. They wanted to have an immediate exchange for our soldiers in Tuzla. At a certain moment, the situation became very serious. There was almost a mutiny of sorts, and the corps commander simply didn't know what to tell them. I happened to be with him at that moment, and he told me this: "Check with your boss," and he meant General Tolimir, "what is going on. When would those 10- to 1.200 captured Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina soldiers arrive?" I picked up the phone, and I got hold of General Tolimir. I asked him when those announced prisoners of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina were to arrive. He told me, "Drop all further preparations. That idea was abandoned, that is, that task." I didn't inquire any further. I simply relayed information to General Simic, the corps commander and then further events took place.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Did he mention to you whether or not they were coming?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC
utterances.text: As I said - perhaps it was not interpreted well - General Tolimir told me, "Drop any further preparations. The task has been abandoned." In our parlance it meant there was going to be nothing that would come out of it. They would not be coming.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: What did you do?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC
utterances.text: I returned from my office and told General Simic that things were not going to proceed, and General Simic was then even more uncertain what to do and what to tell the families of our VRS captured soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Did you have any discussion with General Simic as to what -- what the next course of action was going to be for your corps?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Not at that moment. But the next day, or if it was in the morning, it was later that day, say some 5, 10, or 12 hours later, General Simic called me and he told me this: "I called Lieutenant-Colonel or Colonel Pandurevic, commander of the Zvornik Brigade, and he told me," that's what General Simic was telling me that Pandurevic told him, that there were still members of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina that were trying to break through from Srebrenica to Tuzla, and that capturing them and transporting them to Batkovic was not a problem. In addition to that information, General Simic ordered the following: He told me to organise through the military police battalion for a certain number of vehicles to be sent, as well as soldiers of the military police who were to take over and escort the captured members of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina from the general area of Zvornik to the collection centre at Batkovic. I implemented the order by calling the MP Battalion commander. I conveyed him the corps commander's order. I told him to send an officer with two or three vehicles, as well as a number of military policemen who were to provide security.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: How long after you received the task from the Main Staff was it that you -- how much time passed between the time you received it and the time that you called General Tolimir because the prisoners hadn't arrived?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC
utterances.text: It's a difficult question. Well, not the question but whatever answer I can give you. There must have been at least two to three days. Maybe more.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Could it have been a day or two?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC
utterances.text: I don't think it was as short as only a day or two, because there wasn't -- there wouldn't be enough time for the parents to get all that information and have time enough to pressure the corps command, wanting to know why it wasn't coming about. Well -- but this is just me drawing -- try to draw a conclusion as to a possible time period. I lean towards the figure of two or three days from the moment when the telegram arrived and the instructions to stop preparations.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: When you called General Tolimir, can you tell us how it is you were able to identify that he was the person you were speaking to?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC
utterances.text: I knew it because we knew each other's voices. We met previously and had conversations. It wasn't in 1993 that I met him but a couple of years before that when we closely worked together.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I think this is a good time for the break, Mr. President, if it's time for the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Yes, indeed, it is. We must have our first break now, and we will resume after half an hour, quarter past 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderpuye, before you get the floor, I would like to put a question to the witness. Sir, you explained that you received the order from General Tolimir to prepare for accommodation of the prisoners of war and that you handed this telegram over to your commander. Can you help me: What was the reason why Mr. Tolimir contacted you and not the commander directly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's difficult for me to say anything on that question. It's possible that somebody else from the Main Staff who was supposed to have done that and send that to the general part of the corps command was absent, and so he sent -- so that this was then sent by General Tolimir. In principle, this is not my area of responsibility or part of my assignments in terms of this expert control and direction of the security organs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Again, why did he call you and not the commander, or sent a telegram to you and not to the commander?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't have a concrete answer. I can make an assumption that this would faster along that line of control and that the corps commander would be acquainted with it sooner so that time would not be lost because of the urgent nature of the preparations. This is what I assume, but ... I never thought about anything that I received in the sense of why did I receive it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Your assumption was that Mr. Tolimir stood in for somebody else, another assistant commander, or the commander himself, because they were absent. What did you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, that could have been one of the reasons why General Tolimir signed the telegram, if he signed it. I'm saying "if," because the usual practice with our telegrams -- or, rather, the rule was always to have the chief or the commander sign his full first and last name on the telegram. It can also be signed by a person standing in for them so that the actual, the true signatory can only be seen on the original document that is being archived. The copy that I would receive in the form of a telegram would not indicate the actual personal signature but only it would state, "Deputy -- assistant commander for intelligence and security affairs, General Tolimir." I don't know if he actually signed that himself or somebody else from his sector where he was the chief. I cannot see that from the telegram.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Once again, my question was quite different from what you provided me with. You said perhaps Mr. Tolimir signed this document, this order, addressed to you because other commanders, assistant commanders, were absent. Is that what you are saying?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I did say that, because I'm saying this again now, that it's also possible that he did that because the others were somewhere absent, in the field or on some other assignment, and he happened to be at the Main Staff command post at that time, and as the most senior officer, then he signed that order -- or, rather, that the signature was made on his behalf.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I think you are quite familiar with the responsibilities of the members of the Main Staff. To provide accommodation and prepare accommodation for prisoners of war, whose responsibility in the Main Staff was it to take the necessary steps?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Generally, yes, I am familiar with the duties of certain sectors in the commands from the lowest to the top ones. However, I'm not sure as for the Main Staff in whose sector that would belong. It should be under the assistant for human resources sector and not the assistant for intelligence and security affairs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Who in the Main Staff is responsible for the military police?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The person responsible for the military police in the Main Staff and in the lower-ranking commands in the sense of expert direction and use is the chief -- or, rather, the assistant commander for intelligence and security affairs, and the military police is subordinated directly to the commander. That means that at my level and at the level of the Main Staff as well as at the level of lower commander institutions the chief or assistant commander for intelligence and security affairs proposes to his commander the most rational use of members of the military police, and the commander's word is the last. He decides whether he would accept the proposal in its entirety, some parts of it, or whether he would not accept it at all. Most often the proposal would be accepted, because the assumption is that his assistant is not somebody who's going to be telling children's tales but would provide professional suggestions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I take it from your answer that you have been responsible for the military police in your unit. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] To a certain extent, yes. I was in charge or responsible in the sense that I was overseeing whether the military police unit was executing the ordered and set assignments, and if they were having certain difficulties or hardships, I was there to help them to resolve those problems. Of course, through other colleagues of mine at the corps command. For example, if they were lacking certain supplies, then I would ask the assistant commander for logistics to provide them with what they needed. For example, I would ask him on a priority basis to provide the military police battalion with --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I have to interrupt you. This was a very lengthy answer. I wanted to focus on the chain of command. Who could issue orders to the military police in your unit?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The commander. Exclusively the commander.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Not you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I could if the commander authorised me to do so in certain situations because of an urgent matter, but such situations were rare.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Vanderpuye, please carry on.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I just briefly -- may I just briefly -- for the purpose of clarity, could -- could not -- military police units are issued an order for different assignments. That order is signed by the corps commander. If a plan is made on how to engage forces for a long-term period, then that plan of engagement is drafted by me, but on the left-hand side of the heading of the plan there is a clause stating, "We authorise," and that is signed by the corps commander, which implies that that is his ultimate word in the chain of decision-making. The battalion or some other military police unit is a unit just like any other corps unit. It's subordinated to the corps commander.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Just to follow up on that a little bit, Colonel, can you tell the Trial Chamber whether or not the military police battalion or elements of the corps military police battalion is responsible for securing the Batkovic prison camp?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, they were. A part of the unit from the military police battalion was entrusted for security for the collection centre, or the camp as we refer to it sometimes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And who was in charge of the military police unit that secured the camp at Batkovic in 1995?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Let me just take some time to recollect that. The commander of that small military police platoon at that time I think was Lujic. Yes, Lujic. That is his surname. I can't remember his first name right now. And in that platoon of his or actually that segment of it that secured the Batkovic collection centre were about 20 members of the military police, mostly senior members, who in a way were "given the privilege" of being there because of their age and possible other health difficulties, thus avoiding placing them on some other more demanding assignments elsewhere that perhaps they were not physically up to.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Who would be responsible for providing professional guidance, direction, or control to this military police battalion that was securing the Batkovic camp?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC
utterances.text: It's a part of the military police battalion. That provisionally formed platoon from the military police battalion was practically resubordinated to the warden of the collection centre. As for the professional line and the discipline it was under the control of the military police battalion Captain Major Dragisa Vulin. This platoon commander, Lujic, received his assignments and reported back on the state of security to the komandir, whatever his name was, of the collection centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I'm afraid either there was a translation problem or maybe we've misunderstood one another. In terms of the professional supervision or control over elements of the military police battalion in your corps, was that among your responsibilities as assistant commander for security and intelligence? Maybe that makes it a bit clearer.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. One of the assignments conditionally divided into three spheres, the intelligence sphere that I dealt with, the security sphere or the counter-intelligence sphere, and the military police activities. These three segments made up the activities of my sector.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Up until you received this information from General Tolimir that some thousand or 1.200 or 1.300 prisoners would be arriving at the camp, how many military policemen were stationed at the camp securing it?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC
utterances.text: As for the military police during the preparations, a new contingent was not engaged. The material preparations had just begun, emptying of the hangar and other material preparations in order to be able to receive the prisoners. In the meantime, that activity was halted, and the new contingent, a strengthened contingent of military police from the battalion was never engaged.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Well, how many were there when you got that -- when you were assigned that task? Approximately.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC
utterances.text: As I said before, this was a smaller military police platoon numbering 20 to 25 men that worked in shifts. So on a daily basis 10 of them were engaged while the other 10 to 15 were resting. So they worked in shifts to provide the security. The ones who were engaged on a daily basis had a room where they could sleep so that in essence, possibly -- actually, not possibly, perhaps, you could have two or three active ones. One would be at the reception, the others would be patrolling, and perhaps some others would be in guardhouses in case they were needed.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: From a professional or technical point of view as a security officer or the chief security officer at the corps, would a shift of ten military police be sufficient to secure a thousand to 1.300 prisoners?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Well, no, it wouldn't be sufficient to secure that many prisoners. It would perhaps be the case that the commander, upon my proposal to the corps commander, would receive the task to engage new manpower in order to be able to deal with a convoy and the reception of that number, but that actually never happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And I take it that it didn't happen in this instance because there wasn't enough time for that to happen. Is that fair to say, Colonel?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC
utterances.text: It did not happen solely because further preparations were stopped for their reception. Had the preparations been underway, some other things would need to have been done. As I said, emptying the hangars, providing minimum living conditions, providing additional water taps, providing latrines, providing a place for meals. As I said, this was interrupted after a few days, and all the other activities then were actually never completed.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: With respect to your responsibilities as assistant commander for security and intelligence in the corps, did you have certain concerns or security concerns in relation to the operation of the Batkovic camp?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Of course. Just as in any other kind of organisational units or units subordinated to the corps, I had concerns. I mean, it was my duty and my responsibility to apply methods that were at my disposal as the chief of intelligence and security to acquire timely information and data about the status in the Batkovic collection centre in order to make sure that some secret preparations were not being made for escape, that there was no mistreatment or illegal activity going on. If I were to find out that sort of thing, I would inform the commander and propose measures to him as how to deal with such matters. We never had any serious information about any kind of problem of that nature, however. All the members of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina who had spent a certain amount of time at the collection centre in Batkovic had satisfactory conditions, the situation permitting at the time, that would meet the minimum of their requirements. For example, food was provided from the same sources as food that went to the corps command. That means that we had -- I had the same lunch from the same cauldron that they had their lunch from. Sometimes some supplies would be late in arriving, but that didn't happen very often. This was in the immediate vicinity, so there was never any need for anything like that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. Vanderpuye. I have to put another question to the witness. Sir, you told us all the things to be done before the arrival of the prisoners. This is understandable. What was done before the order came to interrupt these preparations? What had been completed in the meantime?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I remember that a larger hangar had been emptied of the wheat that had been drying in that place. I remember that personnel very quickly gathered all the grain, placed it in sacks and transferred it somewhere else so that that location was emptied so that we could put pallets and mats there for people to sleep on. But the whole activity was suspended when just a small part of all the things that needed to be done was actually done.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Were the pallets and mattresses put into the hangar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. No, they were not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. As long as we're on this topic, could I have, please, in e-court 65 ter 1361. 2686, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Do you recognise what you see on the screen in front of you, Colonel?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC
utterances.text: I do. This is the farm at Batkovic where the collection centre was located.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: What I'd like you to do, if we can, is to mark this photograph so that we can identify the relevant parts of this facility for the Trial Chamber. You had just been discussing a hangar that had to be emptied where some agricultural products -- or agricultural items were held or stored. What I'd like you to do is to mark this photograph with a number 1 where that hangar is.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC
utterances.text: The hangar which was emptied where the wheat had been was this one, I believe. This 1 didn't come out that well, but that's the building.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC
utterances.text: That's where the preparations were begun.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Can you tell us where the prisoners -- first of all, were there prisoners at the facility at the time that the preparations began and, if so, about how many were there?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC
utterances.text: There were approximately between 20 and 30 of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Can you indicate with a number 2 the building or the hangar in which those prisoners were held.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Can you identify from this photograph where the reception area is that you refer to in your testimony.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Of the police, of the military police?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC
utterances.text: This is the way in the compound. This was the gate and guardhouse.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Can you mark that with a number 3 next to what you've just drawn.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Can you tell us what are in the other buildings or what were in the other buildings in 1995 at the time you received this order to prepare to receive the thousand to 1.300 prisoners.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC
utterances.text: I didn't enter all the buildings, but I know that in this building, which lacked some walls, I think it only had a wall on the north-western side, and at the north-eastern side there was no wall. This is where the agricultural machinery was kept. It was a roofed building, though.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Let's mark that, please, with number 4.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC
utterances.text: [Marks] The same, but in this building there were some spare parts for the machinery. It was here. The small building housed their own gas station where they could fill the tanks of their agricultural machines.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Please number those 5 and 6 respectively.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Five is the building where there were spare parts for the machines, and six, I believe, was the gas station for the needs of the farm.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Can you tell us what the long hangar -- what that hangar housed, the one that's in the middle of the screen without a number?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC
utterances.text: It's another hangar with some of the walls missing, if this is the one you have in mind, the one where I placed the dot.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Please number that 7.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And can you tell us about --

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC
utterances.text: It's an open area where there were all sorts of things, anything that might come in handy on such a military farm.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Can you tell us about the building that's unmarked between 2 and 5 as you've marked them on this photograph.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Do you mean this one? I don't know exactly what was inside, but it was in poor condition, so there were no conditions for accommodation in it. The only one which had relatively decent preconditions to house people was the one I marked with 2, which had already been used for that purpose, and we started preparing the building number 1 for the new group.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: The building that you've just -- that you just described and placed a dot, could you number that building 8. This is the one you said you weren't sure of what was kept inside of it.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And in terms of the buildings 1 and 2 that you've marked on this photograph, these were the buildings that were intended to house the prisoners that were supposed to be sent to the camp as per the order of General Tolimir; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. On orders from the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And up until that point, that is, up until you received that order, how many prisoners, roughly, at any given time were held at the Batkovic camp?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC
utterances.text: At the moment when the order arrived, there were between 20 and 30. They were members of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina from the Bihac region, from Western Bosnia. Unfortunately, the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina did not want to consider them for an exchange. They saw the end of the war there. They saw the closure of Batkovic without being exchanged. It was only after the ICRC intervened that they were sent on to third countries so that the entire collection centre could be shut down. There were no other people that -- there at the moment that were of interest. In the building number 2, there could have been up to 400 people accommodated, because these were large facilities where you could line up people in at least four or five rows on makeshift beds that could be used for prisoners. The building number 2 was equipped in that sense. There were beds, blankets and the rest of things that were needed for their accommodation. In previous periods there may have been 30, 40, or 50 people maximum. However, the turnover was rather fast, because there was also an interest on the other side to have such prisoner exchanges conducted quickly.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Just so that -- and before I tender this document, but just so that we have an idea of the size of these buildings, are you able to estimate the size of any one of these buildings, 1, 2, 7? Can you tell us approximately how big it is, that is, how many metres it is, breadth and length? If you can't that's all right, too, but let us know one way or the other.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC
utterances.text: I don't want to just mention a figure and then have to backpedal later. That's not something I want to do. The important thing is that the building number 2 was already used for that purpose, and it could house, at least in my view, between 3- and 400 people. The building number 1 is approximately the same size or slightly bigger. There were newer buildings with good, sound walls and roof, while the rest was almost derelict. It was difficult to use it without some serious reconstruction.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: You mentioned a moment ago ICRC, and I wanted to ask you some questions about that in relation to the prisoners that were kept or detain at Batkovic prison. Could you tell us when prisoners are brought to the Batkovic prison, are they registered -- or were they registered at the time by the ICRC?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC
utterances.text: They were registered at Batkovic upon arrival. Simultaneously, a representative or the office of the ICRC in Bijeljina would be notified. They wanted to be there as quickly as possible, usually within hours, to take part in the registration process.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Mr. President, let me tender this exhibit before I forget.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: This aerial photograph with the markings will be received as an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 65 ter document 2686 marked by the witness in the court shall be assigned exhibit number P2180.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Tell us a little bit about how the ICRC is notified or receives information when a prisoner is brought to Batkovic.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC
utterances.text: The office of the ICRC that existed in Bijeljina was always in contact with the president of the POW exchange commission of the East Bosnia Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And who was that, for the record?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC
utterances.text: It was Major Ljubomir Mitrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Did the security organ at the corps have anything to do with or any contact with prisoners that were held at the Batkovic prison?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC
utterances.text: I didn't have much possibility or opportunity to make a clear distinction or separation of work for my associates between security and intelligence, because we were short of staff. Therefore, it frequently happened that people in charge of intelligence worked on counter-intelligence and my own staff worked on intelligence matters as well. Therefore, members of my security intelligence department also conducted interviews when POWs were received. Those were short interviews. They wanted to know what unit they belonged to, whether they were wounded, and their particulars, nothing more than that. At the end of such interviews, they would share with me such information they obtained through the interviews following the arrival of POWs at the collection centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: What would you do with the information that was brought back to you by your assistants who interviewed prisoners at the camp?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Depending on the nature of that information, because any type of information is used for future assessments, conclusions, and proposals, so it all depended on the type of information.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Did you relay any of the information that you received to the superior security organ at the Main Staff level?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did. Need I explain?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Well, tell us what sort of information it was that you relayed up the security chain.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC
utterances.text: I was under an obligation to send daily reports on security and intelligence support in the corps. That report included three sets of intelligence matters or information. The first set contained intelligence information, that is to say, information about the enemy obtained in various ways, including gathering information from the newly arrived prisoners at the collection centre, for example. Let's say five members of the Tuzla brigade were received at the centre, out of which three were soldiers and one was a commissioned officer and another one was an NCO. I'm just making an example. The first item of the report included intelligence gathered through various methods, not only from the POWs but also from the front lines and through other means that characterized the work of the service. The second set included security issues that may have existed in the units of the East Bosnia Corps, if there were any. The third set included the work and engagement of MP units with all the specific characteristics, issues, if there were any. That was the format of the report. Of course, there's no need and I can't tell you specific information for the 1.000 days that I was there or so. Of course, I informed the corps commander of all that directly through daily briefings in the evening.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Sorry, I have only one question. Sir, you mentioned the name of Major Ljubomir Mitrovic. To which unit did this major belong?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He didn't belong to any unit, but -- can I expand? It takes a bit of explanation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Did he have a superior and, if so, who was it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, you see, it's a specific case in a way. He was directly under the corps commander or under the corps command, but he was an elderly man in poor health who before his appointment to that position was a security organ of the 1st Semberija Brigade.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: His direct superior was the corps commander; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Let me add this: In 1993, when I was appointed to my position, there were certain problems with POW exchanges which had to do with the then president of the POW Exchange Commission. It was then that General Simic, the corps commander, tasked me to find a person appropriate to assume that position who would perform that task better. Taking into consideration the opinion of my subordinates, we concluded that the best available person was Mr. Mitrovic. He used to be a teacher --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I don't need the full record of this person. I just wanted to know who was his superior. I got the answer. Mr. Vanderpuye, please carry on.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He frequently came to my office to consult so as not to go wrong in certain situations. I had the feeling that he did so because he trusted me personally and because I was in a position that was of sufficient importance, and although my rank was junior to the corps commander's rank, he still came to consult with me frequently on certain matters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Did you issue orders to him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: In terms of the information that you relayed to the superior security organ or the organ at the Main Staff, it was the case that you relayed significant information that was conducted as a result of interviews that your personnel carried out at Batkovic. Is that fair?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
