utterances.text: And in addition to your obligation to relay information up the chain, the security chain, you also received instructions to relay within your corps from the Main Staff as concerns the treatment of prisoners of war. Is that fair?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC
utterances.text: In principle, one could say so, although it is something that is regulated by army rules in general. However, occasionally there were situations when instruction was sent in order to draw attention to important issues so as to avoid omissions.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Let me show you P1970. I think you've seen this document before.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: It's a Drina Corps document dated 15 April 1995. You see at the end of the document that it's signed by Vujadin Popovic. First of all, do you recognise the name Vujadin Popovic?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do. My colleague at the same level in the Drina Corps, the same level of duties, the same level post.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And in this document, it refers to the arrest and detention of POWs, and in the B/C/S, on the first page you can see the word "instrukcija," instruction. We can see that in the English on the second page. But on the first page there's an explanation given.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do. I see it towards the bottom of the page, "instrukcija," instruction.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And it says: "Based on the information we received, negligent behaviour has been noticed towards POWs from the moment they are captured to the moment they taken to the Batkovic collection centre or to another place for detention, as well as during the detention itself." It goes on to provide other explanations for what is ultimately an instruction as to how to deal with military prisoners of war. So if we can go to the second page in the English. And if we can scroll a little bit to the left in the B/C/S so we can see the text. We can see under item number 1, hopefully -- I don't know if we can go a little bit --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Item number 1 in B/C/S is on the screen, on the bottom of the page.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I just don't see number 1, and it looks like some of the letters are cut off on my screen, but ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Yes, it is to be seen on the left side.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes. Underneath the "Instruction."

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. We are not able to scroll over so the witness can see?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: The court usher, should we check the Prosecutor's screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. Maybe it's just me.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: We can see under item number 1, it says: "All prisoners, members of the enemy army are to be handcuffed or their hands tied with anything available immediately after their capture." It says: "They are to be searched. All items are to be seized apart from their clothing and footwear." I think we have to go to the next page at some point in the B/C/S. "And an official record is to be completed." Do you see that in the instruction, Colonel?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC
utterances.text: I do, I do. I see it. I'm already -- I've already moved on to the next page.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. That's good. It also says that after the search, "... they are to be blindfolded at the place of detention prior to being led away in order to prevent them from observing anything." In the second paragraph and I won't go through the whole document but in the second paragraph it says that: "The location where POWs are collected must be such --" I see General Tolimir has his hand up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: The microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to greet all those present. I would like to greet the witness. I would like a pleasant stay for the witness. I would like today's day to end according to God's will and not according to mine. And --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the accused please repeat his question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, your comment or question was not interpreted and recorded. Please repeat that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like the Prosecutor either to quote the contents or to avoid retelling them, because then we get the wrong interpretation, and then the witness will probably have the wrong question. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. And I do appreciate the objection, but I am actually reading the text of the English translation, and perhaps that's the source of the confusion if it's being interpreted live, but that's the best I can do since I can't read it in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: And we followed your reading by comparing with the English version. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: In the middle of the second paragraph it reads: "The location where POWs are collected must be such that the prisoners are fully secured, as well as the people from the security organ, from the intelligence organ and the military police organ that engages in the interrogation and guards POWs." First, I just wanted to clarify something with you in terms of this instruction. Is it accurate that the security organ engages in the interrogation of POWs as is certainly suggested in this second paragraph?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Can be engaged if needed or as needed. It's not something that happens always, but the security organ can be engaged.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I want to take you over just to item number 6. That should be on the next page in English and --

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC
utterances.text: I have it in front of me.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. And under item number 6 it says: "In compliance with the estimate of the responsible organ," and then in brackets, "(investigating judge of the military court, security organ, military police commander, military police patrol leader) the arrested person will be transported with his hands tied and with blindfold, or if necessary, with legs tied, especially if there is a danger of escape or if the person is being escorted along the front line through significant elements of the combat disposition; if he is being taken to a position in the unit's combat disposition; or if he is being taken to any significant position in the VRS unit's combat disposition." Do you see that there?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC
utterances.text: I do, yes, and I'm following it. I'm following the text.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. Do you recall yourself having issued or passed on this very instruction within your corps?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Without thinking, I was obliged to pass it on to the subordinate security organs in order to remind them of responsibilities that are regulated anyway. I don't have the right to keep something received from a higher instance only for my own information. That is not the purpose of it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I kindly ask for the heading to be shown to the witness so that we can see who sent the document. He thinks it was sent from the Main Staff, and if the Prosecutor were to ask him whether he passed it on when he received it, then we can see. I mean, did he receive this document at all? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I have no problem with that. We can go to the first page of both documents. I mean both in the B/C/S and in the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: When we look at the heading -- or, rather, I'm sorry, the first paragraph, under "Arrest and detention of POWs," it reads that: "We received a telegram, strictly confidential number 18/20-145-1/94 dated 01.04.1994, from the VRS Security Administration." And then it says: "The telegram outlines in detail the procedure during the detention or arrest of persons violating Rules and regulations. We submit to you the instructions to you in full. Inform military police units with the instruction and act upon the provisions listed." So I'll put this to you, Colonel? Did you yourself receive such an order and pass it on within the corps?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC
utterances.text: I assume that I did, because this is a document drafted by my colleague Vujadin Popovic. It was drafted on the basis of the telegram he received from the security administration of the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska. If I also received it, then it would have been my duty to pass it on and to inform my associates within the department and inform the subordinate military police units and lower-ranking units. When instructions like this are received, they can be sent to all the relevant units, to everybody, or they can be sent only to those units where instances of negligence were observed.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Mr. President -- Mr. President, in light of the witness's answer, I have a document that I'd like to show him. It's 65 ter 7324. It's -- it's a document -- before you load it up --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Can we, before you move to another document, see the last page -- or the bottom of this page in English so that we have a full picture of it. Thank you. We see the last page with the signature of Vujadin Popovic. Mr. Vanderpuye, please carry on.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I was drawing the Court's attention to a document that is on my exhibit list. It was not part of the Prosecution's original 65 ter list, but in light of the witness's answer, I think it would be helpful for the Trial Chamber to see it. I -- I have communicated with Mr. Gajic with respect to some of the documents that are listed on the exhibit list which don't have original 65 ter numbers, so I would obviously ask the Court's leave to show this document. It's hard to show it to you to explain why it's relevant without showing it to the witness, but it is directly relevant to the questions that I've just put to him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Is it included in the list of documents?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: The exhibit list, it is, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: And can you -- now I see, yes. It's 65 ter 7324. Yes. Please carry on with the leave of the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. If I could show 65 ter 7324 in e-court, please. And we'll just look at the first part of it, and then what I'd like to do is to show that next to P1970, just so the Chamber can see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Colonel Todorovic, this is a document as you can see headed -- it says "Eastern Bosnia Corps Command, Security Department." First, that would be your area, wouldn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And you can see from this document that it concerns -- well, first it's dated 20 April 1995, which is five days after the instruction we just saw from the Drina Corps, which is dated 15 April 1995. It concerns --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Could we have a look at the last document again. I was not sure if this is the correct date.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. I'm sorry. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I just want to see --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes. I also noticed the date.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: We can -- we can put it up side by side if that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Just a short look on the previous document.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: It was P1970.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Can we have the English translation of P1970. Thank you very much. It was my mistake. I saw another date. It's fine. This -- the document from the Drina Corps command is dated 15th of April, 1995. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Please carry on.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: In this document, that is the -- that's 65 ter 7324, we see here in the first paragraph a reference to: "Negligent behaviour that has been noticed towards POWs from the moment they are captured to the moment they are taken to the Batkovic collection centre or to another place of detention, as well as during the detention itself." Do you remember having seen this document before testifying here today?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC
utterances.text: You mean this moment?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Yeah. Do you remember seeing it before you've seen it -- you're looking at it now?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I saw it last week while preparing for my testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And was it I who showed you this document?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Does this document contain the same instruction that we saw in the document issued by the Drina Corps chief of security on 15 April 1995 to the subordinate units of that command?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC
utterances.text: It does, yes, except that the introduction with me, my document, is somewhat shorter.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And for you to have passed this information on, you would have had to have received it. That's pretty fair to say, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Correct. That is why my answer a couple of minutes ago I said if I received an instruction or a similar document from my superior command or organ, that does not imply that I acquaint myself with the instruction but inform also my subordinate organs and all the parties in the corps and the corps units. This document is headed "To the 3rd Military Police Battalion," only. So from this you can see that on the original, you can see who signed it and to whom the document was sent. Let's say one brigade of the East Bosnian Corps received this via telegram. The battalion received it directly, because it was some 500 metres away. So it didn't have to be encrypted, but it was just put in an envelope and sent over by messenger, so that the commander of the 3rd Battalion received the original with a proper stamp and signature not via telegram, which is how the colleague from the other corps battalions received it. That is the only difference.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. President, I'd like to tender this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Could we please see the last page in both versions. Sir, do you recognise the signature on this page in B/C/S?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. This is my signature.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And underneath that there is a remark that is handwritten. Perhaps it's a bit hard to read, but it states "Acquainted with," or "informed." The company commander of the armoured transporter unit, Tomic, he was probably standing in for the commander at the time. So to me that is confirmation that the other side received the document on the basis of which they could further act.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderpuye, this document will be received as an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the document 65 ter 7324 shall be assigned exhibit number P2181. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Colonel, in relation to this instruction, we see that on your copy of it, that's just been admitted into evidence, it was directed to the military police battalion of the East Bosnia Corps. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. That is the copy that you are showing, but I do have a comment. Since the battalion command was in the Bijeljina barracks, this document was sent to them directly for purposes of information by messenger. And here, where you can see in the marker written "3rd Battalion of the military police," and then there's a free line, that line is used to note down all the units that are subordinated to me or to the corps command. So other than the military police battalion, the documents were sent to the 1st, 3rd, 5th Brigades and all the other units but you cannot see that from this document. If you had my original document then at the bottom it would state all the addressees to whom the document was sent. But this particular document was only sent to the 3rd Battalion of the military police, but the line, the blank line below the 3rd Battalion would indicate that the document was also sent as a circular to all the other corps units --

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC
utterances.text: -- to be acted upon.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. So this information, this instruction, emanated from the Main Staff security administration, as we can see in P01970. That's the version of the instruction that was passed on by your colleague, Vujadin Popovic in the Drina Corps. And the tasks to which these instructions relate, do -- do they involve the functions of the military police with respect to the treatment of prisoners of war?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC
utterances.text: I don't think I understood your question quite clearly.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Do the tasks that are -- that derive from these instructions, do they have anything to do with the functions of the military police?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, they do.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And you're obliged by your superior in the Main Staff security administration to communicate these instructions to the military police with respect to the handling of prisoners of war; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, and that is this document that we are looking at.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Are you under a corresponding obligation to ensure that tasks over which you have professional control are implemented in accordance with these instructions?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Of course, as is the case with all orders and tasks issued. I mean, if their implementation is not controlled, then there is no point. Otherwise, we will not know if they were carried out, how they are carried out. After each assignment is completed there is control, correction, additions, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: When an instruction such as this one is issued and then passed on through the corps commands to the subordinate units, including the military police, is that done with the expectation that these instructions are -- are met and carried out?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. It is my duty to try to explain one thing. An instruction, that's why I signed it and not the corps commander, does not have the force of an order. It implies the duty to act correctly, professionally, to instruct somebody, teach them, remind them of some duties that are regulated anyway. And for that reason, I signed the instruction and not the corps commander in the sense of instructing the subordinates, reminding them of certain -- actually, not certain but specific duties which are regulated by the rules on the use of military police and so on and so forth, because one of the assignments of military police units is to escort and provide security for prisoners of war, and while escorting and securing them, there are rules as to how this is supposed to be done in order to prevent their violations and negligence. Sometimes it's necessary to issue instructions to remind them of these duties and responsibilities. Sometimes even lectures are held in order to do this.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: The person who receives the instruction, are they duty-bound to follow it?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I think now is a good time for the break, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Yes, indeed. We adjourn and resume quarter past 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderpuye, please carry on.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. If I could have 65 ter 4110 in e-court, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Colonel, I want to show you a document that I hope will be responsive to some of the questions that were put to you by the Trial Chamber as concerns why you received the telegram, as you state, from General Tolimir concerning the prisoners from Srebrenica. This is a document as you can see it's headed -- it says "Command of the Drina Corps, Intelligence Department." It's dated 12 July 1995. And it's addressed to, among other units, your unit, your command, as well as to the intelligence and security departments and directed to the Pribicevac IKM, to General Krstic, and to Lieutenant-Colonel Popovic at the Bratunac IKM. If I could just show you page 2 of this document in both the B/C/S and English. You see at the very top of the page it says: "Chief, Major-General Zdravko Tolimir." Now, what I want to ask you in particular is do you have a recollection of having received this document? Let's start there. If you have a need to look at the substance of it, I can go over some of it with you if that will help you.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC
utterances.text: I briefly looked at the first page while it was still on the screen. However, I believe I should have received it based on its contents, although I can't recall when I received it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please have page 1. The witness asked to see it, I believe.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Yes. There is page 1.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can see it. This document must have been received.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: By you. Correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We can see from the document that it was sent to the adjacent corps, the Sarajevo-Romanija and the Eastern Bosnia Corps to the north and south for their information. As for the tasks, they mainly pertained to the command and units of the Drina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. I just want to go over some of the substance of this document. The first thing is you can see it's dated the 12th of July, 1995. And then you can see that it's directed to the security organs, and about, let's say -- it says in the second paragraph: "On 12th July at 1945 hours, a radio network of elements of the 28th Muslim Division was activated ..." And then it talks about elements of that division came across "our minefield in the sector of Ravni Buljim." If you go to the fourth paragraph it reads that: "Those who communicated over the radio network were extremely frightened and yet undecided about the direction of breaking through the line of defence of the Zvornik Brigade and the 1st -- and the 1st Bratunac Light Infantry Brigade." It says: "In addition to, it's not clear whether all elements of these units had been pulled out from the area of the former Muslim enclave of Srebrenica since they were discovered in the early morning hours after they had activated our minefield." And what I want to focus your attention on in particular is that it says in the next paragraph: "All electronic surveillance units of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps, the East Bosnia Corps and the Drina Corps shall focus on surveillance and monitoring radio communications between these Muslim groups which operate on frequency 164 800." First, from this document it appears that your corps had a surveillance unit capable of monitoring the area in which these individuals were fleeing from the enclave of Srebrenica. Is that -- is that true?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC
utterances.text: The following is true: The command of the East Bosnia Corps had a platoon for electronic surveillance or electronic reconnaissance, which means they used electronic devices to monitor radio networks. They obtained information through such surveillance. However, this doesn't mean that they were capable of seeing physically any of those members. You know how radio waves spread and how they can be intercepted. This task was received, and this was the frequency. It may have changed, but the operators in charge monitored all frequencies. We were under an obligation to inform if we obtained any information even absent this order. We always had to inform our superiors, as I have explained already.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Well, there's two things about this document that I wanted to ask you about. The first is you can see what its subject matter concerns, and that is individuals that are fleeing the area of -- of Srebrenica, and that particular information, from this document it appears to have been communicated to the Eastern Bosnian Corps command and in particular to the security organs. Do you have a recollection of receiving this information on that date concerning these individuals?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC
utterances.text: I said in my answer previously that I must have received this information. There is no reason to doubt that. However, its contents primarily had to do with the units that were along the route the 28th Division members took en route to Tuzla. The part which I understood pertains to me is in this part where it says, "All electronic surveillance units of the SRK, IBK, and DK, shall focus on surveillance." The rest did not have anything to do with the East Bosnia Corps units, because we were at least some 50 kilometres away.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: If we can go to the second page of this document. And if you look at -- I think we have to go also to the B/C/S. If you look at the top of the page in B/C/S and the third paragraph in English, you can see here that General Tolimir states: "Although it is very important to arrest as many members of the shattered Muslim units as possible, or liquidate them if they resist, it is equally important to note down the names of all men fit for military service who are being evacuated from the UNPROFOR base in Potocari." Insofar as this concerns individuals who have surrendered and may be arrested, it concerns, would it not, prisoners of war?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC
utterances.text: One could draw that conclusion, but neither then nor now can I remember my precise role and place in all that. I wasn't in Potocari, and I didn't have anything to do with that part of obligations. I can only draw conclusions based on the document itself. Anything else would be something that is not my direct experience.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. But this is a document, as you said, that you should have received, even though you were 50 kilometres away, as the chief of security of the Eastern Bosnia Corps. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC
utterances.text: That is not in dispute.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I'd like to -- I'd like to tender this document, Mr. President, if I could.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It will be received. Mr. Gajic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, the same document with the same ERN number is already in evidence as D64. It is literally the same.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much for this information.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I'll happily accept that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I had a recollection that I saw this already. The registrar will check if that is the same document. Mr. Gajic, you are absolutely right. It is already in evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Let me just quickly show you -- well, before I show you this document, let me just ask you a question. The date of this document that I've just shown to you now, D64, I think it's referred to now, is 12 July. Is that about the time that you received the information from General Tolimir concerning the arrival of a thousand to 1.300 prisoners at Batkovic?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC
utterances.text: In Belgrade and during proofing a few days ago, I already said that it was in the course of the same few days. I don't know whether it was on the 11th or the 12th or the 13th. In any case it was in that short period.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I think you said a little bit earlier on in the transcript that it was about two or three days after that that you called General Tolimir because the prisoners hadn't arrived. Do you remember that testimony?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do. And I also explained why I called him.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Could I have 1D733, please, in e-court. And we'll need to go to page 40 in the English and page 38, I believe, in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: In your interview on the 2nd of February, 2010, you were asked the following question, and I guess I'll read to put it in context from a little bit -- from probably line 6 or so where you were asked. "Ok, but you said also that it could be the following morning, the following day in the morning." And that's referring to contacting General Tolimir. And you say: "I am really not able to give you an exact answer, not that I don't want to, it's just that I ..." And you were put another question: "Ok, ok, now if I understood you correctly you said it was 24 hours later that you contacted him on the orders of Novica Simic to see what was going on when the prisoners would arrive?" And your answer was: "Yes. Question: "Do you remember that --" Or, rather: "You remember that? "Maybe 24, maybe 48, but quite soon." I understand there is a disparity in the English and B/C/S, but the gist of it is essentially one or two days. Do you see that in your answer to the questions that were put to you during your interview?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC
utterances.text: There is some of what you are asking me about on this page, but I guess the rest spills over to the next page. On this page we have the beginning of preparations.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: On the page in front of you, you will see midway through it, it says, "Da li je 24 ili i vise ..."

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: What does that say so that we're clear for the record. You can read it out.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC
utterances.text: It reads: "Very well. You said that 24 hours later you called on orders by Novica Simic to check what was going on." "Yes. "And where the prisoners were. "Whether it was 24 or more, well, now, two days may have gone by, but shortly thereafter. "So quite shortly thereafter? "Yes. "So it is possible the next day at around the same time, 24 hours? "More than 20." From the moment when the telegram arrived with instructions for preparations until the moment I learned that the preparations were to be stopped. I think it was more than 24 hours. Whether it was two days or three days, that I really can't say. It's difficult for me to say. It's difficult to be precise, to tell you it was at that particular time. You know what conditions we lived under at the time, and frequently we even lost track if it was morning or evening because we had a lot of work to do, and one cannot remember such details, at least not for a long time.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Well, do you stand by what you said in your interview? We can all see it here, so do you stand by it is the question?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC
utterances.text: That's clear. There's no reason for me to change anything. From this interview or from the conversation with you a few days ago I told you that remember the gist of it but I can't recall details. I can't say, decidedly, it was at this hour and this minute. I understand these are big issues, but time takes its toll on my memory. It's difficult. It's not that I don't want to, but, really, I can't. I can't say with full responsibility that it was 24 hours later, 48 hours later. In any case, it was more than one day, because we had already started preparations following the order. The hangar with wheat was emptied, and it could not have been done in five to ten hours. First we had to notify the management of the farm, then they had to bring in the vehicles. So it must have taken at least a day for those things alone, following which we were advised to halt any further preparations. That is why I conclude that it was more than 24 hours. I'm not saying this because I'm certain it was 30 hours, though, or five days.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right, Colonel. Thank you. I want to take you to another area, if I could. I want to ask you a little bit about the Vanikov Mlin prison. Do you know what I'm talking about, first of all?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And can you tell the Chamber where that prison is.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC
utterances.text: That prison is in the town of Bijeljina itself, next to the gate to the military barracks. If you were going that way, to the right would be the barracks and to the left there is the former mill, which was abandoned, and the premises were used to place vehicles and equipment belonging to the military police, and among other things, military detention was in the same building.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And what was the relationship of this prison to the East Bosnia Corps, if any?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC
utterances.text: The military detention unit was an organisational unit of the command of the East Bosnia Corps. It was part of the garrison command, to be more specific. There was the garrison commander who was subordinated to the corps commander. The garrison command dealt with different issues such as housing and health issues ending with the military detention unit. The garrison command was at the helm, and he was directly subordinated to the corps commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Who was the garrison commander in 1995?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC
utterances.text: The garrison commander from 1994 until the end was Lieutenant-Colonel Petar Jovanovic. He died in the meantime.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Did the prison have a warden?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, there was a military prison warden. His name was Milan Savic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Now, you've said that the -- well, let me ask, rather. Was the prison subordinated to the corps commander?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC
utterances.text: I've already said that. Through the garrison commander; it was part of the garrison command. The garrison command is subordinated to the garrison commander and its complete structure.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And you said that it's a military detention unit. What kind of prisoners are held in this facility?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC
utterances.text: The facility held members of the Army of Republika Srpska exclusively due to different reasons, disciplinary violations and violations of military rules.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: The violations of military rules and disciplinary violations, are those matters within the competence of the security organ within the corps in any respect?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC
utterances.text: No. Disciplinary measures for violations are under the jurisdiction of the military commanders.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And with respect to the security facilities or security personnel, rather, at this prison do you have -- or would you have had at the time any professional control as you would over, for example, the military police as the security organ in the corps?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC
utterances.text: The similar applies as for the collection centre in Batkovic. As part of military detention unit, there was a section of the military police which was providing security for the detention area, and my task and role was in overseeing the overall work of the members of the military police. If there was a need, I would also oversee the work of those members of the military police battalion who were providing security in the military detention unit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, could the witness not be asked about professional issues. I mean, by profession he's a military officer. Official duties is one thing. There's a difference between professional duties and official duties. I am just observing that the questions being put to the witness concern his professional position or attitude even though he himself never mentioned that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I think this witness is capable to answer the questions put to him by the Prosecutor, and he may distinguish between different terms, but you may deal with that during cross-examination, Mr. Tolimir. Mr. Vanderpuye, please carry on.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. And if I did make the reference to professional control, I certainly meant it in the context of the specialist control, a professional subordination that the witness had been talking about in his testimony till now.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: You mentioned that the prison was used or that there were exclusively VRS personnel that were prisoners in this prison. Were there prisoners that were detained in this prison that were not VRS personnel?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. As a matter of fact, sometimes at certain points in time they were being brought to the prison premises, to the offices of the military detention facility for informative talks and not to be, conditionally speaking, become the population of that prison. For example, if an interview was supposed to be conducted with somebody who was at the Batkovic collection centre, for example, then there was the option of ordering some of those people by first and last name to be brought to the warden of the military detention unit, to his office, so that one of the security organs, an investigative judge or another authorised person could speak with that person. After that they would be returned to Batkovic. So that was the only way in which from time to time members who were actually -- or persons who were not members of the VRS could happen to be in that building.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Members -- or I should say persons who were not members of the VRS who were there as prisoners would be prisoners of war, wouldn't they?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. There couldn't be anyone else.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And if they were brought to the prison for what you've referred to as a -- informative talks, I just want to clarify what that is. Do you mean by that interrogation or an interview?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC
utterances.text: There was an interview conducted with them. Sometimes on the basis of that conversation, if there were elements there, perhaps an investigating judge would join in this interview, but perhaps if indications were there that it was necessary to conduct an interview based on initial information because one had received this certain or given information.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: When prisoners were brought there, as you said, from Batkovic, for example, to be interrogated, were these prisoners that had already been registered with the ICRC?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And was it the case that prisoners who were brought to this prison -- POWs, I'm sorry, that were brought to this prison had been registered with the ICRC either before being brought there or upon being brought there?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC
utterances.text: They were registered when they entered the Batkovic collection centre. If needed, on the basis of initial information to broaden the interview, then subsequently, so that somebody didn't have to go to Batkovic, there were examples when the warden of the collection centre was called and he was told, "Send such and such a person escorted by the military police to Vanik's Mlin, Vanik's Mill for the purposes of an interview with him."

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: What about prisoners that were brought there who didn't come to Batkovic? Were those prisoners registered with the ICRC at the time they arrived or beforehand? Can you tell us about that?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Well, this is a question that deals with possibilities to which I don't really have any concrete answers. I would like a more specific question, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: When a prisoner is registered with the ICRC, is that something that you as the chief of security would be informed about?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Lists were not in my -- under my authority. I was not supposed to receive complete lists. The president of the Commission for Exchange received complete list, and he would submit a report to the corps commander -- or, rather, he would match up the lists with representatives of the International Committee of the Red Cross at their office in Bijeljina, and the Bijeljina office of the ICRC had unimpeded daily 24-hour access and entrance to the collection centre. So there was no need, nor was it possible for anybody to be concealed who was not registered and who was not in evidence. There's one detail, perhaps I didn't mention it, but for the purposes of clarity of all of this. Besides the ID card -- or the card for each prisoner of war, there was also a register book of all the prisoners of war. When the war was finished and when the collection centre was disbanded, I personally kept this register for some two years at least. I even took it with me out of the premises for fear that it would be lost unintentionally or deliberately, so then later on we would not have any material evidence that things were the way we said they were. And when in Banja Luka, the Government of Republika Srpska drafted records and lists of the total number of casualties and losses, then the register book was handed over to the commission in Banja Luka so that they could have it and compare that record with some of their own lists and records.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Was it the case that there were prisoners brought to this prison, Vanikov Mlin prison, by the security administration of the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC
utterances.text: For a brief period. Perhaps for a day or two or three. After the fall of Srebrenica - and I really cannot tell you the exact dates of the beginning and the end, but in any case, it's the fall of Srebrenica - the team that was conducting the interviews - I think they were from the intelligence sector of the Main Staff - used Vanik mill facilities for these interviews since they're probably -- it's my assumption that they did not have any suitable premises at their disposal in the south, but the registering of these persons was not something that was part of my duties, and they were not obliged to inform me about that, nor did I express any kind of curiosity on that matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I see that we're out of time, so this is a good place to stop.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Yes, indeed. Can you give us an indication about the remainder of your examination-in-chief?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I somehow knew you were going to ask me that. I think I've got three hours and 15 minutes in. I've estimated four, which I think might have been a little bit more conservative than I thought, but I don't think it'll be much more than four anyway, maybe four and a half hours, I hope to finish.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Gajic, we will come back to the discussion at the outset of our hearing today with the reception of number -- of documents and the numbering of them by tomorrow, I hope. We have to adjourn for the day, and we'll resume tomorrow in the morning at 9.00 in Courtroom II. We adjourn.
